caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No. It was carved to win an argument.

In 1868 New York tobacconist George Hull lost a debate at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4 — the verse saying giants once lived on Earth. Angered by the credulity around him, he set out to prove how easily people could be fooled.

With H. B. Martin he hired men to quarry a 10-foot-4½-inch block of gypsum at Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling them it was for a Lincoln monument. The block went to a Chicago stonecutter; two sculptors carved a figure modelled on Hull himself, hanging quilts to muffle the sound. Hull removed the hair, having learned from a geologist that hair does not petrify. Sand and water, sulphuric acid, and steel knitting needles set in a board aged the surface and gave it pores. Cost: $2,600.

Buried behind his cousin William Newell's barn, it was "found" by well-diggers on 16 October 1869. Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute look. Three to five hundred people came a day.

Cornell's Andrew D. White noted there was no reason to dig a well in that spot. Yale's Othniel Marsh called it "a most decided humbug": soluble gypsum still carrying fresh tool marks. Hull confessed on 10 December 1869.

Still unresolved: whether the Chicago stonecutter Edward Burkhardt knew what he was making. And the Michigan arcade that says its Cardiff Giant is Barnum's unauthorised copy — that is its owner's claim, not proven provenance.

Images: the giant photographed by Bain News Service, 1910; the "Onondaga Giant" lithograph, Popular Graphic Arts; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, Fort Dodge, Iowa, from the New York Public Library. All public domain.
